learn.b: The terminal is a text window where you type commands to control the computer. A program called the shell, usually bash, reads each line, runs it, and shows the result. A command is a word followed by options and arguments.

Every shell session is inside one folder, called the working directory. pwd means print working directory and shows the full path. A path like /home/sam/projects starts at the root, which is just a slash.
ls shows what is inside a folder. ls -l gives a long list with sizes and permissions, and ls -a also shows hidden files, which start with a dot. You can combine options, like ls -la.
learn.code:
$ ls
docs  notes.txt
$ ls -a
.  ..  .secret  docs  notes.txt

learn.b: cd changes the working directory. cd docs goes into docs, cd .. goes up one level, cd ~ or plain cd goes home, and cd / goes to the root. A path starting with / is absolute, and any other path is relative to where you are.

qs.q: Which command shows the folder you are currently in?
Which command goes up one folder?
qs.why: Two dots mean the parent folder.

qs.q: You are in /home/sam. What does pwd show after these commands?
qs.why: cd docs moves into the docs folder inside /home/sam.

qs.q: A file whose name starts with a dot is hidden from a plain ls.
qs.why: Use ls -a to see hidden files.

units.title: Files: mkdir, touch, cp, mv, rm

learn.b: mkdir makes a new folder and touch makes a new empty file, or updates the time of an existing one. mkdir -p builds a whole chain of folders at once. You can give several names in one command.
learn.code:
$ mkdir photos
$ touch notes.txt
$ mkdir -p a/b/c

learn.b: cp source destination makes a copy. Use cp -r to copy a whole folder with everything inside. If the destination is a folder, the copy goes inside it with the same name.
learn.code:
$ cp notes.txt backup.txt
$ cp -r photos photos2

learn.b: mv moves a file to another place. If the destination is a new name in the same folder, it renames the file instead. There is no separate rename command in basic bash.
learn.code:
$ mv notes.txt docs/
$ mv old.txt new.txt

learn.b: rm deletes a file for good, with no recycle bin. rm -r deletes a folder and everything inside it, and rm -i asks before each delete. Be very careful, especially with rm -rf, and double check the name.
learn.code:
$ rm old.txt
$ rm -r photos2
$ rm -i maybe.txt

qs.q: Which command makes a new folder?
Which command copies a whole folder with its contents?
What does this command do?
qs.why: mv to a new name in the same folder renames the file.

qs.q: Files deleted with rm go to a recycle bin and can be restored.
Match each command to its job

qs.why: Folder first, then the file, then the copy.

learn.b: cat prints the whole content of a file to the screen. Give it several files and it prints them one after the other, which is where its name comes from: concatenate. It is best for short files.
less opens a long file one screen at a time. Press space to go forward, b to go back, / to search, and q to quit. It does not change the file.

head shows the first 10 lines of a file and tail shows the last 10. Add -n and a number to choose how many, like head -n 3. tail -f keeps watching a file and shows new lines as they appear, which is great for logs.
wc counts lines, words and characters. wc -l gives only the number of lines. It is a handy way to see how big a file is.

qs.q: Which command prints a whole file to the screen?
How do you quit less?
What does this command show?
qs.why: head shows the beginning and -n 3 limits it to 3 lines.

qs.q: tail shows the last lines of a file.
qs.why: tail shows the end, head shows the start.

qs.q: Match each command to its job

learn.b: In ls -l, each file starts with ten characters like -rwxr-xr--. The first says file (-) or directory (d). The next nine are three groups of three: owner, group and others. Each group shows r for read, w for write and x for execute, or a dash if not allowed.

Each permission has a number: read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1. Add them for one group, so rwx is 7, rw- is 6, r-x is 5 and r-- is 4. Three digits give owner, group and others, so 755 is rwxr-xr-x.

chmod also accepts letters. u is the owner, g the group, o others and a all. Use + to add and - to remove. So chmod +x script.sh adds execute for everyone, and chmod o-w file removes write from others.
A script cannot run as a program until it has execute permission. Private files should not be readable by others. Permissions protect your data on a shared computer.

qs.q: What does the x in rwx stand for?
qs.why: x lets a file run as a program.

qs.q: What number is rwx?
What does this command do?
o: Lets the owner, group and others run the file

qs.q: chmod 644 gives the owner read and write, and everyone else only read.
Match each number to its meaning
Type the command that makes script.sh executable for everyone.
Arrange the commands to check a file, make it executable, and check again
Put the three permission groups in the order they appear

lab.q: Challenge: what does the permission string -rw-r--r-- mean?

Only the owner can read it
lab.why: rw- for owner, r-- for group, r-- for others.

learn.b: Most commands print to the screen, which is called standard output. The greater-than sign redirects output into a file instead. A single > replaces the file, and >> adds to the end of it.
learn.code:
$ echo hi > a.txt
$ echo again >> a.txt
$ cat a.txt
hi
again

learn.b: The less-than sign feeds a file into a command as its input. For example wc -l < a.txt counts lines from the file. Many commands can also take the file name directly.
The pipe symbol | sends the output of one command into the next as its input. You chain small tools to do big jobs. Each command does one thing well.
sort puts lines in order and sort -n sorts numbers. uniq removes repeated lines that are next to each other, so sort first. wc counts. Errors travel on a separate stream, and 2> redirects them.
learn.code:
$ sort names.txt | uniq
$ ls missing 2> errors.txt

qs.q: Which symbol sends one command's output into another command?
Which symbol adds output to the end of a file without erasing it?
What does this command do?
o: Counts how many items are in the folder
qs.why: ls output is piped into wc -l, which counts lines.

qs.q: A single > overwrites the file if it already exists.
Match each symbol to its job
pairs: Writes output to a file, replacing it

qs.q: Type the command that saves the word hello into a file named a.txt (use echo and one symbol).

qs.why: Create with >, add with >>, then read.

qs.q: Put the steps of a pipeline in order
items: Second command reads it as input

learn.b: grep searches for text inside files and prints the matching lines. Use grep word file. Useful options: -i ignores case, -n shows line numbers, -v shows lines that do NOT match, and -c counts matching lines.
learn.code:
$ grep error app.log
$ grep -i error app.log
$ grep -n error app.log

learn.b: grep also reads from a pipe, so you can filter any command's output. For example ls -l | grep txt shows only the lines containing txt. Quote text with spaces so the shell passes it whole.
learn.code:
$ ls | grep txt
$ grep "not found" app.log

learn.b: grep -r word folder searches every file inside the folder, including sub folders. It prints the file name before each match. This is a fast way to find where something is written.

find looks for files by name or other facts, not by content. find . -name "*.txt" searches from the current folder for names that end in .txt. The star is a wildcard for any characters. find -type d finds only folders.

qs.q: Which command searches for text inside a file?
Which grep option ignores upper and lower case?
What does this command do?
o: Finds all files ending in .txt below the current folder
qs.why: find searches names, and . means start here.

qs.q: grep -v shows only the lines that do NOT match.
Match each tool to its job

qs.why: Search, count, then filter a listing.

learn.b: echo prints text to the screen. Quotes keep spaces together. echo -n does not add a new line at the end. It is the simplest way to see a value.
learn.code:
$ echo Hello world
Hello world
$ echo "Hi    there"
Hi    there

learn.b: A variable stores a value. Write name=value with no spaces around the equals sign. Read it later with a dollar sign, like $name. By convention, variable names are in lower or upper case letters and underscores.
learn.code:
$ name=Sam
$ echo $name
Sam
$ echo "Hi, $name"
Hi, Sam

learn.b: Double quotes allow variables to be replaced by their values. Single quotes print text exactly as written, with no replacements. Without quotes, extra spaces in a value get lost.
learn.code:
$ n=5
$ echo "n is $n"
n is 5
$ echo 'n is $n'
n is $n

learn.b: $( ) runs a command and puts its output in place. For example today=$(date) stores the date. Environment variables like $HOME and $USER are set by the system, and export makes your variable available to programs you start.

qs.q: How do you create a variable named age with value 14?
qs.why: Bash does not allow spaces around the equals sign.

qs.q: How do you read the value of the variable name?
qs.why: A dollar sign reads the value.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: Single quotes stop the replacement, so the text prints exactly.

qs.q: In bash, name = Sam with spaces around the equals sign is a correct assignment.
Match each symbol to its meaning

qs.why: Assign before using, and re-assign to change.

learn.b: Every command ends with a number called its exit status. 0 means success and anything else means failure. The special variable $? holds the status of the last command. if uses this: it runs its block when the command succeeds.
test checks conditions and the square brackets [ ] are the same thing. Leave a space inside each bracket. For numbers use -eq, -ne, -lt, -gt, -le and -ge. For text use = and !=.
You can test files too. -e checks it exists, -f checks it is a regular file, -d checks it is a directory, and -r, -w, -x check permissions. This is how scripts check before they act.
if condition; then commands; fi. fi is if spelled backwards and closes the block. You can add elif and else. Always leave spaces around the brackets.
learn.code:
if [ $age -ge 18 ]; then
  echo "adult"
elif [ $age -ge 13 ]; then
  echo "teen"
else
  echo "kid"
fi

qs.q: Which word closes an if block in bash?
Which operator means greater than for numbers inside [ ]?
qs.why: Bash uses -gt for numeric greater than.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.code:
age=14
if [ $age -ge 18 ]; then
  echo adult
elif [ $age -ge 13 ]; then
  echo teen
else
  echo kid
fi
qs.why: 14 is not at least 18 but is at least 13.

qs.q: An exit status of 0 means the command succeeded.
qs.why: 0 is success, anything else is an error.

qs.q: Match each test to its meaning
pairs: Exit status of the last command

lab.code:
if [ -e a.txt ]; then
  echo found

lab.why: -e is false, so the else block runs.

learn.b: for name in list; do commands; done runs the commands once for each item. Each time, the variable holds the next item. Items are separated by spaces.
learn.code:
for fruit in apple pear kiwi; do
  echo "I like $fruit"
done

learn.b: {1..5} expands to 1 2 3 4 5. A pattern like *.txt expands to all matching files, so you can loop over files. You can also loop over the lines of a command with $( ).
learn.code:
for i in {1..3}; do
  echo "Round $i"
done
for f in *.txt; do
  echo "$f"
done

learn.b: while runs as long as its condition is true. Something inside must change the condition, or it runs forever. Use ((n = n + 1)) or n=$((n + 1)) for math.
learn.code:
n=1
while [ $n -le 3 ]; do
  echo $n
  n=$((n + 1))
done

learn.b: break leaves a loop right away. continue skips the rest of this round and starts the next. Both work in for and while loops. The loop always ends with done.
learn.code:
for i in 1 2 3 4; do
  if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then
    break
  fi
  echo $i
done

qs.q: Which word ends a for or while loop in bash?
qs.why: Loops open with do and close with done.

qs.q: What does {1..5} expand to?
qs.why: It counts from 1 to 5, both included.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.code:
for i in 1 2 3 4; do
  if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then
    break
  fi
  echo $i
done
qs.why: At 3 the loop breaks, so it never prints 3.

qs.q: A while loop keeps running as long as its condition stays true.
qs.why: Make sure the condition can change.

qs.q: Match each word to its job
pairs: Loops while a test is true

Challenge: arrange the loop that prints each txt file name

lab.q: Challenge: what does this print?
lab.code:
n=3
while [ $n -gt 0 ]; do
  echo $n
  n=$((n - 1))
done
lab.why: n starts at 3 and goes down by one each round until it is 0.

learn.b: A script is a text file of commands that bash runs from top to bottom. It lets you save and repeat work. By convention scripts end in .sh, though the name does not matter to bash.

The first line #! followed by a program path tells the system which program runs the file. For bash scripts write #!/bin/bash. Then give the file execute permission with chmod +x and run it with ./script.sh.
Words you type after the script name are its arguments. Inside, $1 is the first, $2 the second, and so on. $# is how many were given, $@ is all of them, and $0 is the script name.
A real script combines checks, loops and arguments. Check $# first, print a usage message and exit if something is missing. exit 0 ends successfully, and exit 1 signals an error.
learn.code:
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 name"
  exit 1
fi
echo "Hi $1"

qs.q: What does the first line #!/bin/bash do?
o: Says which program runs the script

qs.q: Inside a script, what is $1?
qs.why: $1 is the first word after the script name.

qs.q: You run ./greet.sh Sam. What does it print?
A script needs execute permission to run as ./script.sh.
